overview: Although its name sounds Viking, this imported record is dated 200 to 100 BCE and covers much of southern Norway and Sweden. Those dates belong to the Pre-Roman Iron Age, roughly a millennium before the Viking-age Northmen. The outline should not be read as a proven ethnic border or a united Norse kingdom. Archaeological communities, their farms and their changing skills provide the soundest starting point.

periods.title: The wider Pre-Roman Iron Age
periods.summary: Regional archaeology places this map’s century within a longer period of farming communities before the Roman Iron Age.

sections.title: Norwegian farms, food and useful things

items.text: At Forsandmoen in southwestern Norway, charred grains from the Pre-Roman Iron Age include barley, wheat and oats. Barley dominates the identified grains from this phase, while oats appear toward its later part. Burnt food and crop remains can preserve the agricultural history that ordinary unburnt plants leave behind.

Six Forsandmoen houses of one Pre-Roman type averaged about fifteen metres long and six metres wide. Researchers interpret space for both people and cattle, although the original stall partitions are missing in these houses. Estimates of household and animal numbers are calculations from the available space, not an ancient census.

Forsandmoen’s finds include a curved iron knife from one house, a horse bit from another and complete pottery vessels from two more. Each object adds a different activity to the settlement’s picture: cutting, handling horses and using containers. The assemblage belongs to the broader Pre-Roman period, not one precisely dated year.

A Forsandmoen cairn also preserves evidence that older monuments could be reused. The researcher interprets pottery concentrations as an original early Pre-Roman burial and at least one later burial from the same broad period. A mound could remain important to successive generations rather than serving only one funeral.

sections.title: Swedish farmyards, water and health questions

items.text: At Skälby near Västerås, a 2019 investigation found houses, fences, work areas and wells belonging to one or more farms of the late Pre-Roman and early Roman Iron Ages. The wells place access to water alongside buildings and boundaries in the reconstruction of everyday farm life.

Across Skälby’s longer Iron Age history, wet ground became pasture and hay meadows through work and gradual land uplift. Researchers describe scattered settlement and an important role for livestock. This regional landscape history spans more centuries than the map’s narrow 200 to 100 BCE window.

Some Skälby wells were reused as rubbish pits or places for ritual deposits after people stopped drawing water from them. Archaeologists also asked whether intensive manuring and watering near homes encouraged intestinal parasites. That is a research question in the cited field report, not proof that every household suffered from them.

At Klinga near Norrköping, postholes and hearths helped identify a small Pre-Roman Iron Age farm with a yard. Excavators also recorded cooking pits, a possible well and a pile of cleared stones. Much of this vanished home survives as changes in the soil where its working parts once stood.

sections.title: Communities, craft and the limits of writing

items.text: Two cairns at Sømme in southwestern Norway have been interpreted as ritual constructions connected with settlement expansion and changing landscapes. Their broad date spans the Late Bronze and Pre-Roman Iron Ages. The interpretation reminds us that a heap of stones may have held meanings beyond clearing a field or marking a grave.

For a neighboring comparison outside this outline, the Danish village of Hodde had individually fenced farms inside a common enclosure. At its largest, it contained 27 farms and 53 buildings. Unequal farm sizes suggest differences in wealth within a community that also maintained a shared boundary.

Hodde was occupied for about 150 years before ending around the beginning of the Common Era. Farms moved to another village, and the old settlement ground became fields. This is a local change of land use in neighboring Denmark, not evidence that all Scandinavian communities disappeared together.

Around 100 BCE or shortly afterward, highly skilled goldwork appears in the Nordic region. Fine wires and tiny gold grains were soldered onto ornaments using techniques also known around the Mediterranean. The museum’s comparisons with the Havor and Vittene neck rings illuminate craft connections at and beyond this record’s endpoint.

No securely attested local sentence from 200 to 100 BCE is established by the sources used here. The early runestone fragments from Svingerud in Norway come from contexts dated between 50 BCE and 275 CE, already later than this map interval. Their discovery helps investigate writing’s beginnings without supplying an invented Viking-age phrase for a much older population.

ending.text: The imported 100 BCE endpoint is not a known conquest or extinction. Scandinavian communities continued into the Roman Iron Age, conventionally beginning around the turn of the era, with changing settlements and connections. This broad archaeological record has no single ruler whose fall would explain its ending.
